400.title: Never alone
400.hook: when you shut the door and darken the room, you're not alone: God is within, and your own spirit (Discourses 1.14)
400.carry: a guardian spirit who never sleeps
400.howItsDone: Some readers of Epictetus use this chapter as a nighttime reminder, treating the private, unseen hours as just as real as the public ones.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was adelphos: whoever serves you is kin. Your line was look where your eyes are pointed. And today is day four hundred: four hundred days on the hill.

Late at night, door shut, lights off, phone face down. Nobody can see you. This is the hour when people eat the thing they swore off, send the message they'll regret, or lie awake feeling more alone than they've felt all day. It feels like the one hour that doesn't count, because no one is watching. Epictetus told his students that the dark room is never as empty as it looks.
screen: `DOOR SHUT, LIGHTS OFF.` → `THE HOUR THAT DOESN'T COUNT.` → `THE ROOM ISN'T EMPTY.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter fourteen. A student asks: can a person really believe God sees everything they do? Epictetus answers with the whole world. Everything is bound together. Plants bloom and bear fruit in their season, as if at a signal. Living things change with the moon and the sun. If plants and our bodies are that closely linked to the whole, how much more our minds, which for the Stoics are pieces of the same reason that runs it all. Then the image. God has set beside each person a guardian spirit, a daimon, who never sleeps and can't be fooled. So when you've shut your doors and made it dark inside, never say you're alone. God is within, and your own spirit is within, and they need no light to see what you're doing. For the Stoics, God isn't only someone peering in from outside; God is also the reason in you, never off duty. The chapter ends with a soldier's oath. Soldiers swear loyalty to the emperor, Epictetus says; we should swear one to God too, never to disobey and never to find fault with what we've been given. A neighbor tradition has its own words for the dark. A psalm in the King James words says, "If I say, Surely the darkness shall cover me; even the night shall be light about me." The two aren't the same teaching, and each is held on its own terms. In the psalm, darkness hides nothing from God. In Epictetus, the witness is already inside the room.

Sit in that company, with nothing to hide from it and nothing to perform for it.
Never alone. Epictetus' reminder for the dark room: God is within, and your own guardian spirit, and neither needs light to see.

401.title: Blind, not wicked
401.hook: would you be angry with a blind man? then pity the one blind about good and bad (Discourses 1.18)
401.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners reframe a person who has wronged them as mistaken about what is good, which can soften anger without excusing the harm.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was never alone: the dark room isn't empty. Your line was a guardian spirit who never sleeps.

Someone bumps your cart hard in the grocery store and keeps walking. You turn, ready to say something, and see the white cane. The bump was exactly as hard as it was a second ago, and your shin stings just the same. The only thing that's different is what you now understand about the person. Epictetus asks: what if you understood everyone who wrongs you that way?
screen: `A HARD BUMP IN THE AISLE.` → `THEN YOU SEE THE CANE.` → `WHAT IF YOU SAW EVERYONE THAT WAY?`

segments.voice: Discourses book one, chapter eighteen: that we ought not to be angry with the mistakes of others. Epictetus, the Stoic teacher, starts from something he thinks is true of all of us. Every person agrees with what seems true to them and reaches for what seems good to them. No one does wrong while thinking, this is bad for me, and I want it anyway. So when someone steals or cheats, they've misjudged. They think the stolen thing is good for them, and they're wrong about what's good. That's the whole diagnosis. His students push back. But they're thieves! Robbers! Shouldn't such a person be put to death? Then say it accurately, Epictetus answers. Shouldn't this person, deceived about the most important things, blind, not in the eyes that tell white from black, but in the judgment that tells good from bad, be put to death? Say it that way, and you'll hear how harsh it is. You wouldn't punish the blind or the deaf for not seeing or hearing. Pity them instead. Show them the mistake, and you may see them stop. This doesn't mean pretending harm didn't happen, or that no one should be held to account. Epictetus is talking about anger, the heat inside you. His claim is that the heat rests on a picture of the other person as wicked by choice, and that the picture is usually wrong.

402.title: The clay lamp
402.hook: a thief took his iron lamp, so he bought a clay one, and the thief lost more (Discourses 1.18)
402.howItsDone: Many readers keep Epictetus' clay lamp as a shorthand for letting small losses go: replacing what's gone simply and refusing to give up their own calm or character over it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was blind: the wrongdoer has misjudged what's good. Your line was pity them instead.

Someone takes the package off your porch. Or your bike, or your lunch from the office fridge. It's small, but it stings for days. You replay it, check the doorbell camera, tell five people. Epictetus had something stolen too, and his reaction is one of the most famous little stories in the Discourses: a noise at the window, an empty spot by the shrine, and a cheaper replacement.
screen: `THE PACKAGE OFF YOUR PORCH.` → `IT STINGS FOR DAYS.` → `A NOISE AT THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: It's still Discourses book one, chapter eighteen, right after the teaching about blindness. I kept an iron lamp, Epictetus tells his students, beside the little shrine of my household gods. I heard a noise at the window, ran down, and found it gone. Then I thought it over. The thief wanted a lamp; that's understandable. So tomorrow, I told myself, you'll find a clay one. A person only loses what they have. Notice the arithmetic. An iron lamp was a decent possession; a clay lamp costs very little and gives the same light. Epictetus lost almost nothing that mattered. The thief, as Epictetus sees it elsewhere in the Discourses, paid far more: for a lamp, he became a thief. He gave up his own honesty, which no one could have taken from him, for a piece of iron. Who lost more? Epictetus also explains why thieves make us so angry: we admire the things they take. If you didn't prize your clothes so much, he says, you wouldn't rage at the one who steals them. And there's a funny ending from outside the Discourses. The writer Lucian, a generation later, mocks a man who paid three thousand drachmas for Epictetus' clay lamp after the philosopher died, as if owning it would make him wise. The cheap lamp became an expensive treasure, exactly the kind of admiring Epictetus warned about.

403.title: Not my judgment
403.hook: the tyrant has power over the body, never the judgment (Discourses 1.19)
403.howItsDone: Some Stoic readers sort a fear into what it could touch and what it can't, keeping their attention on their own judgment and choices.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was lychnos, the stolen lamp. Your line was a clay lamp: replace it simply, and keep what can't be stolen.

Epictetus' old master, Epaphroditus, once sold a slave who made shoes, because he thought the man was useless. Then someone in the emperor's household bought the shoemaker, and he became the emperor's own shoemaker. Suddenly Epaphroditus couldn't do enough for him. How is our dear Felicio, he'd ask. Come looking for Epaphroditus, and you'd be told he was in a meeting with Felicio. Epictetus tells it with a straight face, and lets it sit.
screen: `THE USELESS SHOEMAKER.` → `NOW HE WORKS FOR THE EMPEROR.` → `IN A MEETING WITH FELICIO.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter nineteen: how we should behave toward tyrants. Felicio is the joke that opens the door. Why did Epaphroditus suddenly fawn over his old shoemaker? Not because Felicio changed, but because Felicio was now near the emperor. Then the real question. What frightens people? The tyrant and his guards? No. Nothing that is free by nature can be troubled by anything but itself. What troubles us is our own judgments. So when the tyrant says, I'll chain your leg, the person who prizes the leg begs for mercy. The person who prizes their own will says: if it seems better to you, chain it. Take the body, if you have power over it. But no one, Epictetus says, has power over another person's will. They can threaten, and make choosing costly, but the choosing stays with you. Tyrants come in small sizes, too: a boss who controls your schedule, a relative who controls the family's approval, an online crowd that controls how you feel about yourself. The question works on all of them: what exactly can they touch? Your paycheck, maybe. Your mood, only if you hand it over. Your judgment, never. That's not a promise that standing firm will be painless. It's a map of where the fight actually is.

segments.voice: Name one fear that's been pressing on you lately: losing a job, someone's disapproval, a diagnosis, money. Sort it, first what it could touch, my income, my plans, my comfort, my body, then what it can't: what I value, how I treat people, whether I stay honest. Rest your attention on that second list.

404.title: Test the coin
404.hook: test each impression the way a money-changer tests coins (Discourses 1.20)
404.carry: an impression is a coin someone has passed you
404.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners pause on a strong first impression, asking whether it's a fact or an interpretation, before acting on it, a habit some trace to this chapter.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was dogma: the judgments that shape our reactions, out of any tyrant's reach. Your line was the choosing stays with you.

Hand a cashier a hundred-dollar bill and watch. They hold it up to the light, run a pen across it, feel the paper between finger and thumb. Nobody's offended; it's just what you do with money, because fakes exist. Now think how many thoughts you accepted today without holding a single one up to the light. Epictetus noticed the same mismatch in the markets of his own time.
screen: `HELD UP TO THE LIGHT.` → `BECAUSE FAKES EXIST.` → `HOW MANY THOUGHTS DID YOU CHECK?`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter twenty, on reason examining itself. Every skill, Epictetus says, looks at something outside itself: the cobbler at leather, the musician at sound. Reason is the one faculty that can look at itself, and at the impressions that come to it. Then he goes to the market, to the money-changer, whose job is to test coins. For coins, he says, we've invented a whole craft. The tester uses sight, touch, even smell, and last of all hearing: he drops the coin on the counter and listens to it ring. Not once. Again and again, until his ear is as trained as a musician's. Where people think a mistake would cost them, they bring every sense to bear. But the impressions that come to the mind, the passing thought that someone is insulting you, that you're a failure, that you need this thing right now, we accept with a yawn. Epictetus calls this the philosopher's first and greatest work: to test impressions, and let none in untested. An impression is a coin someone has passed you. It might be real. It might be lead painted gold. Before you act on it, say it, or let it set your mood, you can turn it over, hold it to the light, and hear how it rings.
screen: `REASON LOOKS AT ITSELF.` · `THE MONEY-CHANGER'S SENSES.` · `THOUGHTS ACCEPTED WITH A YAWN.` · `HEAR HOW IT RINGS.` · then, large: `TEST THE COIN.`

segments.voice: Let the next thought that shows up be the coin on the counter: a worry, a judgment about someone, a plan. Is it a fact, or a story about a fact? Is it heavier than it needs to be, and does it ring true or a little hollow? Then set it down, and wait for the next one.
Money-changer. Epictetus' image for testing the mind: the market worker who checks a coin by sight, touch, smell and the ring of its drop, before letting it pass.

405.title: A good opponent
405.hook: difficulties show who we are, like a trainer pairing you with a rough young wrestler (Discourses 1.24)
405.carry: what is this making of me
405.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners reframe a difficulty as a training partner, asking what virtue it calls on, a habit drawn from this chapter's wrestling image.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was money-changer: test each thought before you spend it. Your line was an impression is a coin someone has passed you.

In a boxing gym, the coach looks over the new kid and pairs him, on purpose, not with the easiest partner but with someone a little rougher, a little stronger, someone who makes him sweat and sometimes puts him down. He goes home sore and annoyed. A few months on, he moves differently. Epictetus took that gym wisdom and pointed it at the hardest things in life.
screen: `THE COACH PAIRS HIM ROUGHER.` → `SORE AND ANNOYED.` → `A FEW MONTHS ON.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter twenty-four, on how to struggle with circumstances. It opens with a short line: it's difficulties that show what people are. Then the picture. When a difficulty lands on you, Epictetus says, remember that God, like a wrestling trainer, has paired you with a rough young opponent. Why? So that you can become an Olympic champion, and that doesn't happen without sweat. Then something bold. No one, he tells his student, has ever been handed a better difficulty than yours, if you're willing to use it the way an athlete uses a tough sparring partner. Notice what he's not saying. Not that the difficulty is good in itself, or that you deserved it, or that suffering is secretly pleasant. The opponent is rough. It hurts. What he changes is the question. Instead of, why is this happening to me, he asks: what is this making of me? A sparring partner isn't your enemy, even when he puts you on the mat. He's how you find out what you've got, and how you get more of it. For the Stoics, the trainer is God, the reason that runs the world. Some readers keep that, and some keep only the gym. Either way, a hard conversation, a setback at work, a stubborn habit can be read as the partner your training needed.

406.title: Stand firm
406.hook: the good lies in the will, so stand firm there (Discourses 1.29)
406.carry: let the branches move in the wind
406.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners prepare for pressure by naming in advance what could be lost and what couldn't, and anchoring themselves in their own choices.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sparring partner, the rough opponent a trainer chooses for you. Your line was what is this making of me. Today ends the week.

A tree in a storm doesn't stay still. The branches thrash, leaves tear off, the whole crown bends sideways. What keeps it standing is underneath, out of sight: the roots, gripping the ground. A tree that tried to hold every leaf in place would snap. Epictetus has a whole chapter on constancy, on staying steady when pressure comes, and his advice runs the same way as the tree's. Know where your roots are.
screen: `A TREE IN A STORM.` → `BRANCHES THRASH, ROOTS HOLD.` → `KNOW WHERE YOUR ROOTS ARE.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter twenty-nine, on constancy. It opens with a short, dense claim. The good, Epictetus says, is a certain state of the will, and so is the bad. Everything outside the will, money, health, reputation, even the body, is material the will works with. Earlier in the Discourses he puts it this way: as wood is the carpenter's material, each person's own life is the material of the art of living. The carpenter isn't good because the wood is fine, but because of what he does with it. That's where the roots are. If your good lives in your will, pressure on everything else is weather in the branches. A threat to your job, your comfort, your standing: those are leaves, real and worth caring about, but not the roots. Then Epictetus imagines the test. Someone powerful threatens you. Don't panic, he says; ask what is being threatened. If it's the body or the property, the will is still standing. He even pictures God calling a student forward as a witness: come and testify for me. Is anything outside the will good or bad? Will you show up and say it, or tremble and say the opposite? Constancy isn't stiffness, or refusing to feel the wind. It's knowing which part of you is supposed to move and which isn't. The week in a breath: never alone, blind, not wicked, a clay lamp, not my judgment, test the coin, a good opponent, and now stand firm.
screen: `THE GOOD IS A STATE OF THE WILL.` · `EVERYTHING ELSE IS MATERIAL.` · `CALLED FORWARD AS A WITNESS.` · `NOT STIFFNESS: KNOWING THE ROOTS.` · then, large: `STAND FIRM.`

segments.voice: Feel your feet flat on the floor, the ground solid under you. Let one pressure blow through like wind, a deadline, a hard conversation, someone's expectations, and notice what bends: plans, comfort, mood. Then come back to your feet, and to what doesn't need to bend: what you value, how you mean to act.
Stand firm. Epictetus' constancy: the good lives in the will, so let the branches move in the wind and keep the roots where they are.
Your line: let the branches move in the wind. The roots are yours. Day four hundred six, and the week is whole.
